clue.text: Bird of prey taking young mammal and beginning to eat

parts.note: a kit is the young of a fox, ferret or similar small mammal

indicators.note: beginning to says only the opening letter of the next word is used

explanation.surface: A hawk swoops down, seizes a baby animal and starts its meal.
explanation.definitionFit: The kite is a fork-tailed raptor, so it is a bird of prey by kind.

clue.text: Musically, Nelson's last request redirected?

parts.note: Admiral Nelson is said to have died asking 'Kiss me, Hardy'; send the same request to a different person and you have the title of a Cole Porter musical

explanation.walkthrough: Nelson's famous dying words were 'Kiss me, Hardy'. Redirect the request from Hardy to Kate and you get the Cole Porter stage musical based on The Taming of the Shrew.
explanation.definitionFit: A Cole Porter musical whose title is a plea for a kiss, like the admiral's reported dying words.

clue.text: Checked shirt perhaps fastened round back of collar

indicators.note: round says the phrase for fastened goes around another letter

parts.note: tied on means fastened with a knot or string

indicators.note: back of says the final letter of the next word is used

explanation.surface: A tartan shirt with something fixed around the back of its collar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Checked' looks like a pattern, but here it means tested: you check a shirt's fit when you try it on.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothing is put on in a shop to check that it fits, so a shirt so tested has been worn briefly.

clue.text: Pool, large craft wrecked — here one has to stay

indicators.note: wrecked says the letters are smashed up and put back together in a new order

parts.note: pool and craft are taken as written, with large giving L, its standard abbreviation as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A big boat has come to grief in a pool, and its passengers must remain there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrecked' scrambles POOL, L and CRAFT together.
explanation.definitionFit: A port of call is a place where a ship or traveller stops for a while on a journey.

clue.text: Took extra pill? Skilful swallowing the same

parts.note: a pill is slang for a ball, and a ball is round like the letter O

indicators.note: swallowing says one word takes the other into its middle

parts.note: versed means skilled or knowledgeable
do is short for ditto, meaning the same again

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a pill-taker overdid it, then praises their skill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pill' is not medicine but old slang for a ball, hence the round letter; 'the same' is ditto, abbreviated.
explanation.definitionFit: To overdose is to take more of a drug than is safe, an extra dose.

clue.text: Settlements never in easterly direction?

definitions.meaning: ... and villages are settlements where people live
heading west, north or south, every compass point except east

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the answer into TO W, N, S: three compass directions, with E left out, so never heading east.
explanation.definitionFit: Small urban places where people have settled are municipal communities, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: In market, squander a possibility? Honestly!

parts.note: a fair is a market or show where goods are sold

indicators.note: possibility suggests one possible arrangement of the letters, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone at a market fears wasting an opportunity and exclaims in exasperation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibility' rearranges SQUANDER A into AND SQUARE, which follows FAIR.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something squarely and fairly means doing it honestly, without cheating.

clue.text: Stern dismissal, having lost head in game regularly

indicators.note: in says the shortened word sits inside the picked letters
regularly says every other letter of the word is taken
having lost head says the opening letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: an ouster is a removal from office, a dismissal

explanation.surface: A harsh sacking during a match, after which someone is beheaded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having lost head' turns OUSTER into USTER, which goes 'in' A and E, picked 'regularly' from 'game'.
explanation.definitionFit: A stern manner is severe and strict, which is what austere means.

clue.text: Connection is left fluid

parts.note: ink is a writing fluid

explanation.surface: A statement that some relationship remains flexible and unsettled.
explanation.definitionFit: A link joins two things, so it is a connection.

clue.text: One lying on the beach slightly reduced illness

indicators.note: slightly reduced says a small part, one letter, is cut from the end

parts.note: shingles is a painful viral illness causing a rash

explanation.surface: A sunbather whose illness has eased a little.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One lying on the beach' suggests a sunbather, but it is the pebbles themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: Shingle is the mass of small pebbles found on many British beaches.

clue.text: One kindly rescuing merchandise waving at airman

parts.note: goods are merchandise for sale

indicators.note: waving suggests movement, so the letters are shaken into a new order

explanation.surface: A pilot waves while someone kindly saves the cargo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'waving' rearranges AT AIRMAN into SAMARITAN, after GOODS.
explanation.definitionFit: In the parable, a Samaritan stopped to help a robbed traveller; the phrase now means any kind helper.

clue.text: A little decent weather for the holiday?

parts.note: a whit is a very small amount, as in not a whit
sun is pleasant weather

explanation.surface: Hoping for a spell of fine weather over a bank holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: Whitsun, or Pentecost, was a traditional British bank holiday weekend.
explanation.definitionFit: Whitsun is the Christian feast of Pentecost, long marked by a public day off in Britain.

clue.text: Very keen detectives have no trouble going round to subdue killer

indicators.note: going round says the joined words surround another

parts.note: mad about something means extremely keen on it
DIs are Detective Inspectors
ease is freedom from trouble or difficulty
to cow is to intimidate or subdue

explanation.surface: Eager police find it easy to overpower a murderer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going round' makes the joined pieces split so that the verb for subdue lands between the first and second words.
explanation.definitionFit: BSE is a fatal brain disease of cattle, deadly to animals and, through its human form, people.

clue.text: Captain's top shirt lent out — it wouldn't cover many soldiers

indicators.note: out suggests the letters are thrown out of order and reassembled
top says only the first letter of the word is used

explanation.surface: An officer lends out his best shirt, which would not fit many soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges C (Captain's top) with SHIRT LENT.
explanation.definitionFit: A slit trench is a narrow foxhole dug for one or two soldiers, too small for a group.

clue.text: Men promoted two books in a number of colleges

definitions.meaning: in draughts, a man reaching the far row is crowned and becomes a more powerful piece
the Old Testament contains First and Second ...
several colleges bear this name, at Cambridge and in London among others

explanation.surface: Staff promotions, two volumes and several universities listed side by side.
explanation.walkthrough: Three definitions: draughts pieces, two Bible books, and colleges named King's.
explanation.definitionFit: Crowned pieces in draughts, two Bible volumes, and several colleges named for a monarch.

clue.text: Plant to propagate satisfactorily, fed with phosphorus

indicators.note: fed with says one word has another put inside it

parts.note: to seed is to propagate plants from seed
P is the chemical symbol for phosphorus
well means satisfactorily

explanation.surface: Gardening advice: a plant grows well when given phosphorus fertiliser.
explanation.definitionFit: Speedwell is a small flowering herb with blue flowers, a common wild plant.

clue.text: Embracing lover-boy after change of heart is certain to be raised as wrong

indicators.note: embracing says one piece wraps around the other
in a down clue, raised says the word is written bottom to top

parts.note: sure means certain

indicators.note: change of heart says the middle letter of the word is swapped for another

parts.note: Romeo is the archetypal young lover

explanation.surface: A girl changes her mind about her boyfriend and is sure she was wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: ROMEO's heart M becomes N, giving RONEO; SURE 'to be raised' gives ERUS, which is 'Embracing' it.
explanation.definitionFit: Erroneous means mistaken or incorrect, a synonym of wrong.

clue.text: A month in Rome, third on the trot

indicators.note: on the trot suggests running about, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A horse comes third in a race in Rome during a certain month.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the trot' rearranges ROME and THIRD.
explanation.definitionFit: Thermidor was the eleventh month of the French Republican calendar, in high summer.

clue.text: What's in vintage wine, a little more than old

indicators.note: a little says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Fine wine is described as being a bit more than merely old.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit inside 'more than old'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethanol is the alcohol produced by fermentation and present in every wine.

clue.text: Leave empty ring

indicators.note: ring is read as a verb, to encircle, so the word for leave surrounds the letter

parts.note: to quit is to leave
empty means having nothing in it, and nothing is O

explanation.surface: An instruction to walk away from an empty arena.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ring' does double duty: QUIT rings O (zero, for 'empty'), and the whole clue describes the thing itself, a hollow ring that is let go.
explanation.definitionFit: A quoit is a hollow ring of rope or metal thrown at a peg, released from the hand.

clue.text: House, too big, subsequently managed

indicators.note: subsequently says the second piece comes after the first

parts.note: OS is the abbreviation for outsize, meaning too big
borne means endured or coped with, as in managed

explanation.surface: A house proves too large, and later someone copes with it.
explanation.walkthrough: Osborne House on the Isle of Wight was Queen Victoria's seaside home.
explanation.definitionFit: A famous royal residence, so it is a stately mansion, the sense meant here.

clue.text: An aid to exercise: dash, maybe

definitions.meaning: a gymnast's apparatus for swinging and pull-ups
a dash in punctuation is a short level line

explanation.walkthrough: One sense is gym equipment; the other is a typographical dash, a flat stroke.
explanation.definitionFit: Gymnastic apparatus and a level stroke of punctuation are both described by this phrase.

clue.text: Pound and a fraction raised by area

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised says the letters are written bottom to top

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for pound, from the Latin libra
an ounce, OZ, is a fraction of a pound, so a fraction gives AN OZ

explanation.surface: Money and a small share collected locally.
explanation.walkthrough: L plus AN OZ, 'raised', reads upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Zonal means arranged by zones, that is divided by area or region.

clue.text: Lamb no longer first for roasting in vessel

parts.note: a female lamb that has grown up is a ewe

indicators.note: first for says the opening letter of the following word is used

explanation.surface: Mutton, not lamb, is put in a dish for roasting.
explanation.definitionFit: A ewer is a large jug, a kind of container for water.

clue.text: Statesman no defeat broke? Almost

parts.note: a win is a result that is no defeat

indicators.note: almost says the word stops one letter short of its end

parts.note: stony, as in stony broke, means having no money

explanation.surface: Asking whether a politician who avoided defeat was nearly bankrupt.
explanation.walkthrough: STONY, from 'stony broke', loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Winston Churchill, Britain's wartime Prime Minister, is the statesman known by this first name.

clue.text: Heavily defeat old guard finally wiped out by king in battle

indicators.note: wiped out by says one letter is removed and the next replaces it

parts.note: Verdun was a long First World War battle in France

indicators.note: finally says the last letter of the word is taken

parts.note: R is short for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: An elderly sentry falls to a monarch in combat, routed.
explanation.walkthrough: Verdun (1916) was the longest First World War battle; 'wiped out by' swaps its D, the last of 'guard', for R, giving VERRUN.
explanation.definitionFit: To overrun an enemy is to defeat it thoroughly and occupy its ground.

clue.text: Corps fast reduced, cuts being this?

parts.note: RE stands for the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
Lent is the Christian period of fasting
less means reduced or smaller in amount

explanation.surface: Army spending cut back again; are these cuts unending?
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the question at the end: cuts that keep coming, as in austerity.
explanation.definitionFit: Unremitting cuts that never ease are described as unrelenting or unceasing.

clue.text: Old Testament character prepared hard

parts.note: set means ready or prepared
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A biblical figure who was ready and tough.
explanation.definitionFit: Seth was the third son of Adam and Eve, a figure in Genesis.
